h1: Laser welding machines — handheld welders from 0.8 kW, robotic cells to 20 kW, laser cladding
intro: A fiber laser welder joins stainless, aluminum, galvanized and mild steel sheet with a narrow, deep seam at five times the speed of TIG, with almost no heat distortion and no grinding afterwards; handheld, it takes a day to learn, and on a robot it runs the same weld all shift. NovoTech sells Senfeng laser welding equipment in Canada: the portable air-cooled S series at 0.8 to 1.5 kW on wheels, the HWM handheld welders at 1.5 to 3 kW with wire feed for joints to 9/32″, robotic laser welding cells from 1.5 to 20 kW with positioners and tracks, teaching-free and collaborative MIG robots, and the laser cladding machines that rebuild shafts, rolls and bores with a metallurgically bonded wear layer. Senfeng makes its own sources and heads in Jinan, China; CE / FDA / ETL certified. Installed and supported from Mississauga, ON, Canada.

faq.q: What can a handheld laser welder do that TIG cannot?
faq.a: Speed and heat. A 1.5 kW laser welds 16 ga stainless at 10 – 15 in/min with a seam that needs no grinding, puts a fraction of the heat into the part — thin sheet, boxes, cabinets and railings stay flat — and welds dissimilar thicknesses, galvanized and aluminum that TIG struggles with. An operator who has never welded produces clean seams after a day of training. It does not replace MIG on heavy plate: the 3 kW HWM welds 9/32″ mild steel in a single pass and the robotic 6 – 20 kW cells go to 9/16″.

faq.q: S series or HWM — which handheld welder?
faq.a: The S series is the portable machine: 0.8, 1.2 or 1.5 kW, air-cooled with no chiller, 99 – 121 lb on wheels and a 220 V single-phase plug — for a shop that moves it between jobs or takes it on site. The HWM is the production welder: 1.5, 2 or 3 kW with a water chiller, a 33 ft cable, a wire feeder and the 4-in-1 head that welds, cleans the weld, cuts sheet and seam-welds — for a station that welds all day and for joints to 9/32″.

faq.q: Is it safe to use in a shop?
faq.a: A class 4 laser needs a controlled area: the welders ship with a CE face shield, laser-resistant gloves and clothing, and the gun fires only with the safety clamp on the workpiece. We recommend the welding booth with laser-protective glass for a fixed station, and fume extraction as for any welding. Operator training is part of the installation.

faq.q: When does a robot make sense?
faq.a: When the same joint is welded hundreds of times a day: tanks, frames, boxes, exhaust, furniture. The RW laser cells run 1.5 to 20 kW on a 6-axis robot with a positioner so the seam is always in position; the CMW cobot is the simplest entry — a 350 or 500 A MIG torch on a collaborative arm, programmed by guiding it by hand over the part, on a cart you wheel to the job; the RMW scans the part with a camera and writes its own program, for batches of one.

faq.q: What is laser cladding used for?
faq.a: Repairing and hardening: worn shafts, hydraulic cylinder rods, rolls, valve seats, pump housings and dies get a new wear- or corrosion-resistant surface — stainless, nickel, cobalt or carbide alloys from powder — fused to the base metal with a thin heat-affected zone, far stronger than thermal spray and with less distortion than overlay welding. Layers to 25/64″ (10 mm), machined afterwards. Mining, oil and gas, hydro, pulp and paper and steel mills are the usual customers.

faq.q: What does the machine need on site?
faq.a: The S series plugs into a 220 V outlet; the HWM, robots and cladding machines run on 3-phase — we supply the transformer for 600 V. Shielding gas (argon or nitrogen), compressed air for the cutting and cleaning modes, a fume extractor, and for the cladding machines a powder supply. Delivery, installation and training by NovoTech from Mississauga, ON, Canada.

faq.q: What voltage do these machines run on?
faq.a: Three-phase machines are supplied for 600 V as standard with a CSA-approved panel; 208 V, 240 V and 480 V 3-phase are available on request, and 240 V single-phase on models whose main motor is 2.2 kW (3 HP) or less — a machine with a motor above 2.2 kW must run on three-phase power and cannot be converted to 240 V single-phase. Manual machines have no electrics.
